title: Test water with found kits
summary: What pool, spa and aquarium kits, pH strips, TDS meters and bacteria and lead kits can and can't tell you about drinking water, and the free-chlorine check after you chlorinate. The kits here can't show fuel, solvents, most chemicals, viruses or parasites, so a kit is a check on good treatment, never a reason to drink doubtful water.

materials.item: Pool or spa test kit that reads free chlorine (DPD) and pH
pH strips or a calibrated pH meter
Aquarium test kit for ammonia and nitrate
Clean glass jars, a marker and a notebook
Disposable gloves for handling untreated water

steps.text: Check the kit: expiry date, no damp or discoloured strips, reagents capped. Chlorine must be a DPD (pink) test for free chlorine, not an OT (yellow) one, which reads total chlorine only (Taylor FAQ).

Put on disposable gloves and eye protection before you open any reagent, and keep reagents capped, in their own bottles and away from children. Taylor's DPD reagent #1 irritates eyes and skin (Taylor R-0001 SDS), and API's pond-kit ammonia solution #2 contains bleach and sodium hydroxide and burns skin and eyes (API ammonia #2 SDS). Rinse a splashed eye with water for several minutes, and pour a tested sample out: it is not drinking water.

Test the untreated water first and write the readings down with the date and place: pH, nitrate, ammonia and TDS if you have the kits. These tell you about the source, not whether it's safe (HC well test).
Read nitrate in the chart's own units. Over 45 mg/L as nitrate (10 mg/L as nitrate-nitrogen), the water isn't for babies or formula (HC nitrate).
steps.warn: Boiling doesn't remove nitrate (HC nitrate). Find another source for infants.

steps.text: Read ammonia before you add any bleach: free chlorine reacts quickly with ammonia and uses it up (ADWG ammonia). Most uncontaminated source water is below 0.2 mg/L, and over 10 mg/L has been reported where animal waste got in (ADWG ammonia). A high reading is a reason to move upstream or choose another source, but a normal one clears nothing: some deep wells in certain geology carry a lot of ammonia (HC ammonia TD).

Note the TDS. A sudden rise at a source you know can mean road salt, sewage or other pollution got in (VT TDS). A normal reading doesn't clear germs or many organic chemicals, pesticides among them (HM Digital TDS).

Clear cloudy water, then disinfect it. WHO wants turbidity under 5 NTU before chlorinating (WHO TN11): see [Clear muddy water with alum](#guides/skill_settle_with_alum) and [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters).

Wait the full contact time: at least 30 minutes at 18 °C or warmer (WHO TN11). Colder than 10 °C, or cloudy: HealthLinkBC doubles the bleach and lets it stand one to two hours before drinking (HealthLinkBC 49b); WHO only says longer when colder (WHO TN11).

Test free chlorine. For a treated batch, WHO's drinking-water guidelines ask for at least 0.5 mg/L free chlorine after 30 minutes at pH below 8 (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO). That shows the dose wasn't all used up; it doesn't prove the water is safe (WHO TN11, Health Canada chlorine TD).

No free chlorine, or under 0.5 mg/L: add the same dose again of plain unscented bleach, wait 15 minutes more and test again (EPA water, HealthLinkBC 49b). Still none: settle or filter it better, or use another source.
A blank or faint reading on water you dosed heavily may be bleached reagent: dilute 1 to 1 with chlorine-free water, test, and double the result (Taylor FAQ).

If the pH reads above 8, chlorine works more slowly (Health Canada chlorine TD). MSF's cholera guidance waits 60 minutes and wants 1 mg/L free chlorine, against 30 minutes and 0.5 mg/L at pH 8 or lower (MSF cholera).

For a bacteria kit, fill the vial straight from the source or a running tap without touching the inside, and wait the full time, often 48 hours. Read the result against your kit's own colour key: yellow meant positive in the kits San Francisco tested (SFPUC kits), but in LaMotte's kit yellow without gas bubbles is negative (LaMotte 4-3616-UV). Chlorine left in a sample can hold back growth and give a false clean result, so don't test freshly chlorinated water unless the kit includes a dechlorinating tablet (LaMotte 4-3616-UV).
steps.warn: A negative bacteria test doesn't rule out viruses, Giardia or Cryptosporidium (HC E. coli). Boil or filter surface water anyway.

steps.text: Treat a used bacteria vial as a culture. LaMotte's kit says to add about 1 mL (1/3 teaspoon) of household bleach to each tube, recap at once, leave it about 4 hours, then throw it away without opening it again or cleaning it for reuse; wash your hands afterwards (LaMotte 4-3616-UV).
Don't trust a lead kit's negative: most can't see lead at drinking-water levels (Kriss 2021). Treat old plumbing as a lead source.

notes:
## What each kit can and can't tell you
| Kit | Tells you | Doesn't tell you |
|---|---|---|
| Pool and spa kit, DPD (turns pink) | Free and total chlorine, so whether a chlorine dose has done its job. Most also read pH (Taylor FAQ) | Germs or chemicals: only whether chlorine is left over |
| Pool kit, OT (turns yellow) | Total chlorine only (Taylor FAQ) | Free chlorine, the part that disinfects (WHO TN11) |
| pH strips or meter | Acid or alkaline. Chlorine works best below pH 8 (Health Canada chlorine TD); acidic water pulls more lead and copper from pipes (HC pH TD) | pH itself has no direct health effect (HC pH TD), so a good pH clears nothing |
| Aquarium kit (ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH) | Signs of manure, sewage or fertiliser (below). Read by colour card (API master kit) | Germs, metals, fuel |
| TDS meter | How many charged particles (salts and minerals) are dissolved | What they are, germs, fuel, many pesticides (HM Digital TDS, VT TDS) |
| Bacteria kit (colour change after about 48 h) | Coliform bacteria, a sign of sewage or animal waste (SFPUC kits) | Viruses and parasites (HC E. coli) |
| Lead kit | Yes-or-no strips can show dissolved lead (Kriss 2021) | Lead in particles; most kits can't see lead at drinking-water levels (Kriss 2021) |

A kit is a check on a source you chose well and a treatment you did properly. It is never a reason to drink water you'd otherwise refuse: see [Choosing the safest water source](#guides/reference_water_sources).

## The chlorine check after treating
This is the test that matters most, and a pool kit does it.
- **Wait the full contact time first.** WHO: at least 30 minutes at 18 °C or warmer, longer when the water is colder (WHO TN11). Colder than 10 °C, or cloudy: double the bleach and let it stand one to two hours before drinking (HealthLinkBC 49b); EPA doubles it for very cold water too, with no temperature given (EPA water).
- **Read free chlorine, not total.** Free chlorine is what is left to kill germs once the water's chlorine demand is used up; combined chlorine has reacted with nitrogen and no longer disinfects (WHO TN11).
- **Target:** WHO wants 0.2 to 0.5 mg/L where people collect water (WHO TN11), but that range is for water collected from a supply, and the 0.2 mg/L minimum in Health Canada's document is a pipe-network figure it quotes from others (Health Canada chlorine TD). For a batch you've just treated, WHO's guidelines ask for at least 0.5 mg/L after at least 30 minutes at pH below 8 (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO 2004), and MSF wants 1 mg/L above pH 8 (MSF cholera). So aim for at least 0.5 mg/L after the wait. Above about 0.6 to 1.0 mg/L, more people find the taste off (Health Canada chlorine TD); to soften it, pour the water between clean containers and let it stand a few hours (EPA water).
- **No reading?** Repeat the dose and wait 15 minutes more (EPA water), then test again. A reading means the dose wasn't all used up. It doesn't prove the water is safe: chlorine residuals are expected to leave Giardia and Cryptosporidium unaffected (Health Canada chlorine TD), can't reach germs inside silt, and remove no chemicals (WHO TN11).
- **Still nothing after two doses:** the water is eating chlorine. Let it settle longer or [clear it with alum](#guides/skill_settle_with_alum), and find the dose with a bucket test (IFRC jar test).

For water, 1 ppm is 1 mg/L (HM Digital TDS). If your bleach is old, [test its strength](#guides/test_bleach_strength) before dosing.

## Reagents are chemicals
Wear gloves and eye protection when you open reagents; keep them capped, in their own bottles and away from children. Taylor's DPD reagent #1 is classed as causing serious eye and skin irritation (Taylor R-0001 SDS). API's pond-kit ammonia solution #2 contains sodium hypochlorite and sodium hydroxide and causes severe skin burns and eye damage (API ammonia #2 SDS); your own kit's label says what is in your bottles. For a splash in the eye, rinse with water for several minutes (both SDSs). A sample with reagent in it isn't drinking water: pour it out, and keep leftovers away from bleach, acids and cleaners (see the [chemical card](#browse/hazards/chemical)).

## Reading strips and drops well
- Use the printed expiry date, and keep reagents and strips at 2 to 29 °C, out of sun, capped (Taylor FAQ). A kit that froze in a truck or cooked in a shed is suspect: check it on a known dose as the [water test kit part card](#browse/parts/det_water_test) describes.
- Strips and colour comparators are only good to half the gap between two colour blocks; drop-count tests to one drop, about 10% (Taylor FAQ).
- Above about 10 ppm, chlorine can bleach DPD to a false low or zero. Dilute the sample 1 to 1 with chlorine-free water, test, and double the result (Taylor FAQ).
- Chlorine over 10 ppm also upsets the pool kit's pH test (Taylor FAQ).
- San Francisco's 2018 to 2019 trial of three home-kit brands rated their pH results poor to mixed and their total chlorine results mixed, and called kit results an initial step, not a final result (SFPUC kits).
- Test at the same spot each time and write the readings down with the date: a change at a source you know tells you more than one reading.

## Nitrate and ammonia: signs of sewage and manure
**Nitrate** comes from farming, sewage, industry and traffic (HC nitrate), and Health Canada links it to farms and domestic sewage in wells (HC well test). The limit is 45 mg/L as nitrate, which is the same as 10 mg/L as nitrate-nitrogen. Aquarium and test-strip charts use one or the other, so read which. Bottle-fed babies are most at risk: water over the limit isn't for formula or babies' food, and boiling doesn't reduce or remove nitrate (HC nitrate). Conventional treatment (settling, filtering, chlorinating) doesn't remove it. Residential reverse osmosis can bring it lower and ion exchange can be used, but how well either works has to be checked, so test the output before it goes near an infant (HC nitrate); another source is safer: see [12 V reverse osmosis](#guides/build_ro_12v). Shallow wells in farm country are particularly prone to it (HC nitrate).

**Ammonia** forms from urea in human and animal excrement, so it can flag pollution. Most clean source waters have less than 0.2 mg/L, and over 10 mg/L has been found where animal waste got in (ADWG ammonia). It reacts quickly with free chlorine (ADWG ammonia), so ammonia-laden water uses up chlorine and turns it into the combined kind: expect to need more bleach before free chlorine shows. So an aquarium kit's ammonia test on untreated water is a rough pollution screen (ADWG ammonia calls ammonia an important pollution indicator): a high reading is a reason to move upstream or choose another source, but some deep wells in particular geological settings have high ammonia and a low reading clears nothing (HC ammonia TD).

## TDS meters
A TDS meter is a conductivity meter: it measures how well the water carries a current and converts that to parts per million with a factor, usually about 0.5 to 0.7 (HM Digital TDS, Hanna TDS). Only charged particles conduct (USGS conductivity), so it reads dissolved salts and minerals. HM Digital, a meter maker, lists what it won't see: uncharged compounds such as sugar, alcohol, many organics including many pesticides, un-ionised ammonia, silica and carbon dioxide; particles such as rust or anything that makes water cloudy; and bacteria and viruses (HM Digital TDS). It can't name what it does read (HM Digital TDS, VT TDS).

What it is good for: road salt, seawater, mine and sewage pollution raise TDS (VT TDS), so a jump at a source you've measured before is a warning. A reverse osmosis unit or still should give a lower reading than what went in (our inference, no source tests it), but a low reading doesn't make water safe: the meter can't see bacteria, viruses or many organic chemicals (HM Digital TDS). The US aesthetic limit is 500 mg/L, set for taste, not health (VT TDS).

## Bacteria kits
In San Francisco's trial of three brands, coliform results agreed with the lab more than 80% of the time, yet SFPUC calls kit results an initial step, not a final result, and recommends a certified lab for follow-up (SFPUC kits). How to get a fair result (SFPUC kits, LaMotte 4-3616-UV):
- Don't touch the inside of the vial or the water; don't cough or sneeze over it.
- Fill it straight from the source or a running tap, not from a jug or cup.
- Wait the full time on the kit, often 48 hours. Read it against your kit's own colour key. In the kits San Francisco tested, yellow, sometimes with gas bubbles, was positive; in LaMotte's kit both yellow and gas bubbles are needed for a positive, and yellow alone is negative (LaMotte 4-3616-UV).
- Chlorine left in a sample can hold back growth and give a false clean result: don't test freshly chlorinated water unless the kit comes with a dechlorinating tablet (LaMotte 4-3616-UV).
- A used vial is a culture. LaMotte's kit says to add about 1 mL (1/3 teaspoon) of household bleach to each tube, recap at once, leave it about 4 hours, then throw it away without opening it again (LaMotte 4-3616-UV).

E. coli in a sample is a good sign of recent faecal contamination (HC E. coli), so a positive means treat or move. A negative doesn't clear the water: E. coli testing alone can't confirm whether disease germs are present, and E. coli dies sooner and is more easily killed by chlorine than Giardia, Cryptosporidium and many viruses (HC E. coli). Health Canada wants wells tested for bacteria at least twice a year (HC E. coli).

## Lead kits
In a study of 16 brands of home lead kits, 12 couldn't detect lead below 5 to 20 mg/L (Kriss 2021), 1,000 to 4,000 times Health Canada's limit of 0.005 mg/L (HC lead). Simple yes-or-no strips did detect dissolved lead at levels that matter, but missed lead in particles; in that study, lemon juice or vinegar dissolved some of the particles so the strips picked them up (Kriss 2021). San Francisco rated home lead results mixed (SFPUC kits). Treat any old plumbing as a lead source whatever a kit says: see [Water in a building](#guides/reference_building_water) and the [lead card](#browse/hazards/lead).

## What these kits can't tell you
- **Fuel, solvents and fire chemicals.** The only way to know if water holds benzene or other VOCs is a lab analysis (EPA wildfire VOCs). Water that fuel or toxic chemicals may have reached can't be made safe at home (CDC find water).
- **Most chemicals.** Many contaminants don't change the smell, taste or colour of water, and only an accredited lab or public health unit gives reliable results (HC well test). Chlorine doesn't remove chemicals; that takes specialist knowledge and equipment (WHO TN11).
- **Most pesticides.** The pesticide kits San Francisco tried named atrazine and simazine, were rated mixed, and gave one false positive that the lab disproved (SFPUC kits); a TDS meter misses many pesticides (HM Digital TDS).
- **Viruses and parasites.** No kit here detects them; a clean coliform result doesn't rule them out (HC E. coli). Chlorine leaves Cryptosporidium and Giardia alive (Health Canada chlorine TD): boil or use a cyst-rated filter for surface water.
- **Blue-green algae toxins.** See the [blue-green algae card](#browse/hazards/cyanobacteria).
- **Water that is never for drinking.** A reading on water from a heating loop, boiler, antifreeze, hot tub, waterbed or sprinkler system means nothing: that water isn't for drinking at all. See [Water in a building](#guides/reference_building_water).
